title: The pianist as band leader: chords, reading and playing solo
summary: Thompson explains that the pianist supplied chord progressions for ear-playing horn men, and that playing solo made him able to lead and prompted him to write music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Well, Sir Charles, why don't you go on. You were telling us about your experiences in the CC Camp, and then how you would go into the town and play there, and come to know the visiting bands, and eventually you had an offer and you just had reached the point where you were going to join up, and why don't you tell us what happened after that?
Well, yes, I -- this band leader,

Cecil Scott, well, as I said, you know, when you go and play, guys like you're playing, and the musicians, you know, in a musician's world, you learn to play with someone else who can play or who can interpret your music, or can help you interpret. And a pianist in particular, especially in those times, more so than now, there weren't that many piano players who could play this music right. And the piano was more or less the leader of the group if you believe it or not because they depended on you playing the right chord progressions for them to hear what they were to play. Because of the musicians played strictly by ear.

Now, that doesn't mean that they couldn't read notes, because they read notes -- when you read an orchestration for the benefit of those who know music or even if you don't know music, when you play an orchestration, that's what you're doing. You're playing something that was written by someone else, and if you're playing in a large orchestra with more than one instrument, or several instruments, you're playing a part, like in a choral group like when you sing. You sing parts. There's a lead part and there's an alto part, a tenor part, the base part, so on, like a quartet. Same thing. You have parts.

Now, so you're reading the notes of the parts, the same as a piano player. The piano player is reading some notes and chord progressions, and like, you know, et cetera. But the thing about it is when you're playing ad lib you're

playing the chord progressions (which means) that you're leaving reading notes now and you're thinking in your head what chord is this I am to play in each one or two bars, a half a bar, or so many beats, and what not have you.

And so the piano player was like the leader because he had to play the right chord for them to hear what they were playing. And some of the musicians who didn't know these chords so well, they had the perfect pitch as I was speaking of, they could hear, believe it or not, what chord to play. You see?

But the greatest musicians, the ones who were the leaders, like I mentioned before, like Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge and many other great jazz players during that time, they were proficient inasmuch as they could read music, sight read music, and they could play chord progressions. And they were ahead of everybody else in that department. And most of the piano players who played, who were well versed, who had any kind of training at all, knew these chords. They didn't necessarily have to be good piano players but they knew the chords.
In my case, I happened to be, which I will have to associate with my competitive feeling and spirit, as well as a desire to learn and a desire to want to be a part

of something, I was able to play the right chords and play solo. And having played solo piano by myself gave me the power and the strength and the knowledge to play with other people, and I was able to lead the other players as well as the boss players and the horn players, because my feeling was so strong and definite, in other words I knew what I was trying to do, and then I was always the type of person -- I never liked to do anything if I don't know what I'm doing. And I would try to learn the right chords to the piece. If I didn't I'd go and buy the music or learn it from someone who knew it.

Which started me into my interests of writing music, because I wanted to learn, you see. But I still hadn't learned enough what I was learning, but I played well enough to be complimented by these musicians and to be wanted to replace this other piano player.
